channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] France seeks EU sanctions on Iran over refrigeration sabotage as Iran-linked hackers turn to physical attacks on industrial controls
item.description: France asked its EU partners on 16 November to sanction those it blames for the October sabotage of refrigeration at about 700 French sites, and Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said he expects measures at the 14 December foreign ministers’ meeting, with backing from most member states. Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit and has sought arrest warrants for three officers; Iran calls the accusations baseless. The case fits a wider shift: US and Israeli officials told the Wall Street Journal on 13 November that Iran-linked hackers have moved from data theft to sabotaging equipment, locking operators out of small Midwest water stations and breaching networks aboard two Texas-bound energy tankers. The weak point is still open: Germany’s BSI and Belgium’s CCB warned on 13 November that Danfoss AK-SM 800A controllers carry six unpatched pre-login flaws. Treat any internet-reachable controller as a proven target. - Asharq Al-Awsat and The New Arab (16 Nov 2026, EU sanctions push); Wall Street Journal (13 Nov 2026), via Newsmax wire on Yahoo News and Voice of Emirates; RFI via AOL (11 Nov 2026, Paris prosecutor’s warrant request); Insurance Journal, from Reuters (13 Nov 2026, BSI warning); Bytes Europe (13 Nov 2026, CCB warning); Midnight Blue (Nov 2026, AK-SM 800A research); GBHackers (13 Nov 2026); NPR (9 Nov 2026, Iranian denial); Iran International (14 Nov 2026, IRGC response); Arab News, from AFP (12 Nov 2026, Belgian statement) - EU sanctions push 16 Nov 2026; WSJ report 13 Nov 2026; BSI and CCB warnings 13 Nov 2026; warrant request 11 Nov 2026; French attribution 9 Nov 2026; IRGC rejects French findings 14 Nov 2026; October attack 11–12 Oct 2026; investigations ongoing

item.title: [Critical] CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
item.category: Incident — CISA/FBI/HHS/USDA/DOT joint warning (5 Nov 2026) and a second wave of refrigeration attacks across about 11 European countries (1–4 Nov); Belgium says its evidence points to Iran (12 Nov), no formal attribution
item.description: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers in European supermarkets, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French stores were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost, and three French blood-service sites had settings changed with no blood lost. On 10 November Sweden warned that more incidents are likely after refrigeration was tampered with at seven Coop stores and an undisclosed number of ICA stores on 2 November; its NCSC says the victims mainly ran older systems from one manufacturer protected by weak passwords. On 12 November Belgium’s interior minister said evidence on the Belgian attacks points to Iran but stopped short of an official attribution (see top story); a pro-Russian claim is unverified, and France has formally attributed only the separate 12 October attack, to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. Exposure is falling but not gone: exposed Danfoss StoreView instances dropped from 3,004 to 708 between 9 October and 5 November (The Hacker News, 9 November). Sekoia reported on 10 November that the second wave used a non-public, unauthenticated flaw that renames the controller’s admin account, apparently a step towards resetting its password, and assesses that both waves may come from the same actor. If a controller is reachable from the internet, treat it as at risk today. - TechCrunch (5 Nov 2026, CISA/FBI joint statement); SentinelOne Labs (3 Nov 2026, updated 4 Nov); Cybersecurity Dive (3 Nov 2026, updated with 4 Nov developments); Unit 42 (6 Nov 2026, exposure counts); Censys (6 Nov 2026, exposure analysis); BleepingComputer (5 Nov 2026); Nextgov (29 Oct 2026); Al Jazeera (4 Nov 2026); CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-ALE-012; The Cyber Express (6 Nov 2026, CISA/FBI/HHS/USDA/DOT advisory summary); Industrial Cyber (6 Nov 2026); Help Net Security (6 Nov 2026); SecurityWeek (6 Nov 2026, hardening guidance); The Hacker News (9 Nov 2026, exposure trend); eBuilder Security (11 Nov 2026, Swedish government and NCSC warning); Arab News/AFP (12 Nov 2026, Belgian statement); Sekoia TDR (10 Nov 2026, second-wave technique) - Attacks overnight 1–2 Nov 2026; Germany, Romania and UK confirmed 4 Nov 2026; CISA/FBI joint warning 5 Nov 2026; French attribution of the October attack 9 Nov 2026; Swedish government warning 10 Nov 2026; Belgian minister points to Iran 12 Nov 2026 — investigations ongoing

item.title: [Critical] Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
item.category: Incident — PHP2Shell plus Gaia root flaw CVE-2026-123039 used to backdoor Check Point gateways and wipe a VMware ESXi host (wave 1 from 30 Oct, Israel; wave 2 from 2 Nov, multiple countries); CVE-2026-123039 added to CISA KEV 13 Nov 2026
item.description: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, about a week after fixes shipped, then used a local flaw in the gateway’s DynamicCLI service (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted web shells and backdoors named TSGA and TSProxy, scanned the internal network, moved over SSH to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper that overwrites and deletes files. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached gateways in several countries and sectors with no destruction seen. The backdoors resemble tooling linked to the China-nexus group UNC5221, but Check Point does not attribute the campaign with confidence. CISA added CVE-2026-123039 to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these firewalls often sit at the IT/OT boundary and ESXi hosts often run HMIs and historians (editorial assessment). - Check Point Research (12 Nov 2026); SecurityWeek (13 Nov 2026); Canadian Centre for Cyber Security AV26-1154 (12 Nov 2026, updated 13 Nov); CISA KEV alert (13 Nov 2026); BleepingComputer (Nov 2026) - Wave 1 from 30 Oct 2026; wave 2 from 2 Nov 2026; research published 12 Nov 2026; KEV addition 13 Nov 2026

item.title: [Critical] PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
item.category: Active exploitation — PHP2Shell chained with a Linux kernel flaw to root exposed PAN-OS firewalls, 23–24 Oct; OT vendor advisories 28–30 Oct
item.description: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified on 29 October that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to gain root on about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October, then stole Active Directory credentials. Victims were in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea. The OT exposure widened: Siemens now lists Spectrum Power grid-control systems and AMIS TS, Schneider lists a Foxboro DCS server, and ABB lists Netcontrol RTUs and ASPECT gateways, several with no fix yet. Attribution is suspected, not confirmed, and no Siemens, Schneider or ABB product is reported exploited. No OT operator has been named, so treat this as an IT-to-OT boundary warning. - Unit 42 (updated 29 Oct 2026); Palo Alto Networks advisory for CVE-2026-109618 (updated 29 Oct 2026); The Record (29 Oct 2026) and Infosecurity Magazine (30 Oct 2026), citing Dream; CISA KEV catalog (30 Oct 2026 release); Siemens SSA-166980 V1.2 (29 Oct 2026), SSA-566512 V1.1 (28 Oct 2026), SSA-019113 and SSA-082556; Schneider Electric SESB-2026-295-01 v3.2.0 (30 Oct 2026); ABB Netcontrol and Arctic advisories (30 Oct 2026), ASPECT advisory (29 Oct 2026) and APROL SA26P015 (23 Oct 2026); CERT@VDE VDE-2026-127 and VDE-2026-137 - Root compromises 23–24 Oct 2026, verified by Unit 42 29 Oct 2026; KEV additions 26 and 28 Oct 2026; Siemens, Schneider and ABB updates 28–30 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] A malicious update to drone ground-control software disrupted operations at German defence supplier Quantum Systems, reports say
item.category: Incident — Supply-chain compromise reported at German drone maker Quantum Systems via a malicious QBase ground-control software update (detected late Oct; reported 13 Nov 2026); no attribution
item.description: Quantum Systems, a German maker of military reconnaissance drones, says it detected an incident in late October that was part of an active attack by “hostile actors,” and that it worked with authorities so its unmanned systems could safely resume operations. Der Spiegel and the Financial Times, citing internal sources, report that the attackers pushed a malicious update to QBase, the company’s ground-control and mission-planning software, from the vendor’s own update server; it is unclear how many customers installed it. The German armed forces reportedly grounded the company’s drones as a precaution and left them out of a recent exercise. The company believes it was targeted for supporting Ukraine but names no attacker. For OT owners the lesson is wider than defence: a vendor’s update channel for control or engineering software is a direct path onto operational systems (editorial assessment). - BleepingComputer (13 Nov 2026), citing Der Spiegel and the Financial Times and a Quantum Systems statement - Incident detected late Oct 2026; reported 13 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] Brazil’s Port of Santos, Latin America’s largest, confirms a cyberattack that knocked its online systems partly offline for days
item.category: Incident — Port of Santos (Brazil) authority confirms cyberattack on its systems; online services partly down since 6 Nov 2026, Federal Police inquiry opened 10 Nov
item.description: The Santos Port Authority (APS) confirmed on 10 November that its systems had been hit by a cyberattack, after online services had been partly unavailable since a power interruption on Friday 6 November. Internet and telephone service came back on 9 November after about three days, and the authority said other services were being restored gradually with no date for full recovery. It has not yet established how far the intrusion reached or whether data was accessed, and Brazil’s Federal Police opened an investigation the same day. Port operations continued, but some administrative work moved to alternative procedures, which slowed parts of the cargo flow. No group has claimed the attack and no link to the power interruption has been confirmed. The affected systems are reported as administrative rather than terminal or crane control; for ports, that is still how a business-side outage turns into berth and gate delays (editorial assessment). - Jornal do Comércio, from agency reports (10 Nov 2026, APS confirmation and Federal Police inquiry); BNAmericas (11 Nov 2026); Port Continuity Brief (15 Nov 2026, citing CNN Brasil) - Systems disrupted from 6 Nov 2026; attack confirmed 10 Nov 2026; recovery ongoing

item.title: [Medium] Maersk confirms hackers took data from an old logistics system it inherited, as the WhiteArmor gang demands $5 million
item.category: Incident — Maersk confirms data theft from a legacy logistics system inherited through an acquisition (11 Nov 2026); WhiteArmor ransomware group claims about 100 GB and demands $5 million (unverified)
item.description: Shipping group Maersk confirmed on 11 November that an attacker reached a local legacy system it inherited through an earlier acquisition and extracted data, after the WhiteArmor ransomware group listed the company on its leak site. BleepingComputer links the system to LF Logistics, which Maersk bought in 2022. Maersk says the incident is isolated to that one system, with no sign that other Maersk systems or customer and partner API and EDI connections were affected, and it expects no disruption to bookings or shipments. WhiteArmor claims about 100 GB, including driver records, plaintext passwords and 33 super-admin accounts, and has set a 30-day deadline. Maersk says current evidence shows no sensitive data disclosed. Inherited systems from acquisitions are a recurring blind spot: they often keep their own credentials and connections long after the deal closes (editorial assessment). - BleepingComputer (11 Nov 2026, Maersk statement); GovInfoSecurity (Nov 2026); Cybernews (Nov 2026); Industrial Cyber (Nov 2026) - Leak-site claim weekend of 8–9 Nov 2026; Maersk confirmation 11 Nov 2026; investigation ongoing

item.title: [High] Volt Typhoon has used a rotating “Silent Train” relay network since 2023 to break into management platforms, with water, energy and transport among the victims, Lumen reports
item.category: Threat Intel — Lumen Black Lotus Labs report (28 Oct) on Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” relay network and zero-day campaigns against management platforms; water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail and aviation among victim sectors; no OT intrusion described
item.description: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs reported on 28 October that Volt Typhoon has used “Silent Train”, a covert network of rapidly rotating, single-use chains of compromised small-office routers, IoT and enterprise devices, since November 2023 to reach targets and keep access to management and control-plane systems. Lumen ties the group to four confirmed zero-day campaigns and one likely one: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS v3.1 10.0, Cisco), VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812), N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876), Versa Director (no CVE given) and, with moderate confidence, Quest KACE (no CVE). These are older flaws, not the VeloCloud flaw CVE-2026-114625 that CISA added to KEV on 23 October. Victims include telecoms, government, defence contractors, IT firms and MSPs, and universities, and Lumen lists water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation and emergency services among the critical-infrastructure sectors hit; Hawaii, California and Texas recur as focal points (Zero Day). No victim is named and no OT or ICS intrusion is described. Lumen points defenders to CISA’s Volt Typhoon guidance (AA24-038A) and its advisory on China-nexus covert networks (AA26-113A). Management and orchestration platforms often hold trusted paths into plant networks, which makes them the asset to protect here (editorial assessment). - Lumen Black Lotus Labs (28 Oct 2026); CyberScoop (28 Oct 2026); Zero Day (28 Oct 2026); CISA KEV catalog - Report published 28 Oct 2026; activity tracked since November 2023

item.title: [High] Hijacked Copeland XWEB refrigeration controllers are relaying spam and proxy traffic, and one intrusion pushed setpoints to 150 °C
item.category: Research — hijacked Copeland (formerly Dixell) XWEB PRO refrigeration controllers used as spam relays and proxy exits (SecurityScorecard STRIKE); separate setpoint-tampering intrusion of 2 Nov 2026 (Ransom-ISAC); reported 9 Nov 2026
item.description: SecurityScorecard’s STRIKE team reported on 9 November that internet-exposed Copeland XWEB PRO controllers, which run supermarket freezer and chiller racks, are being abused as spam relays and proxy exits; one unit in Trinidad and Tobago contacted more than 10,000 hosts in 17 hours. It suspects CVE-2026-25085, a login-bypass flaw among the 23 that Claroty Team82 reported and CISA published in February (ICSA-26-057-10), but has not confirmed the entry route. Separately, Ransom-ISAC analysed a 2 November intrusion in which attackers simply used the factory default administrator login, read settings on 31 devices and made 743 changes, including setpoints of 110 and 150 °C, muted alarms and locked keypads. Neither team links its findings to the Iran-attributed European attacks, but a second refrigeration platform is now being actively abused (editorial assessment). - SecurityScorecard STRIKE and Ransom-ISAC, via Help Net Security (9 Nov 2026); CISA ICSA-26-057-10 (Feb 2026, Claroty Team82 disclosures) - Tampering intrusion 2 Nov 2026; research reported 9 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] Unpatched GeoVision camera-management software gave cryptominers a way into 13 organizations
item.category: Threat Intel — Huntress: attackers exploited unpatched GeoVision GV-VMS camera-management software at 13 organizations, mostly 8–10 Nov 2026, to deploy cryptominers; fixed release V17.4.8.58 available
item.description: Huntress reported on 16 November that attackers broke into 13 organizations through internet-facing GeoVision GV-VMS video-management servers, mostly between 8 and 10 November, and used the access to run cryptocurrency miners. The affected hosts ran an older build (17.4.8.0); GeoVision’s April 2026 advisory lists three unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaws in the WebCam Server component for that build, and Huntress has not yet determined which one was used. A fixed release, V17.4.8.58, is available. The victims’ sectors were not named. Camera and access-control servers often sit on facility and building-management networks next to OT, and a miner today can be a foothold for something worse tomorrow (editorial assessment). - Help Net Security (16 Nov 2026); Huntress threat advisory (Nov 2026) - Intrusions mostly 8–10 Nov 2026; reported 16 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] SANS survey: OT incidents up 1.7× in a year, and leaders are far more confident than engineers that plants can run without IT
item.category: Research — SANS 2026 ICS/OT survey (696 practitioners plus a smaller leadership sample), reported 12 Nov 2026
item.description: The SANS 2026 ICS/OT survey found that 34% of respondents had an industrial cyber incident in the past year, 1.7 times the 2025 rate and the biggest one-year rise SANS has recorded, and 72% of those incidents caused downtime. Fewer were caught quickly: 41% were detected within 24 hours, down from more than half in the two previous years. The sharpest gap is in resilience. Every security leader surveyed expected their plants to keep running through a full IT compromise, yet only 15% of practitioners said critical processes could run safely by hand for more than 48 hours, and 40% did not know. Only 16% have fully folded OT into business-continuity planning, and 68% said losing one or two veteran staff would slow response or create serious operational risk. Dedicated OT detection platforms caught more incidents (38%) than any other method, but budget remains the main barrier to wider deployment. For defenders, the practical point is to test the manual-operation assumption before an attacker does (editorial assessment). - SANS Institute 2026 ICS/OT survey, via Help Net Security (12 Nov 2026) - Reported 12 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] Six unpatched pre-login flaws in Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration controllers prompt Belgian and German warnings to pull them off the internet
item.category: Advisory — Six pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaws in Danfoss AK-SM 800A (firmware up to 5.3.2), disclosed by Midnight Blue; Belgian CCB and German BSI warnings, 13 Nov 2026; CVEs pending; no exploitation of these flaws reported
item.description: Amsterdam consultancy Midnight Blue has disclosed six stack buffer overflows in Danfoss AK-SM 800A system managers, the store-level controllers that run supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration, that allow remote code execution without logging in; one works even with “strict” session control turned on. All firmware up to 5.3.2 is affected and CVEs are still pending. The BSI says the 5.4.0 package released this month is not affected, but Midnight Blue says 5.4.0 predates its research and does not fix these bugs, so treat 5.4.0 as unconfirmed until Danfoss says otherwise. The researchers say an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset or firmware update, or brick units, because the device does not appear to use secure boot; that is a stated possibility, not a demonstrated one. On 13 November Belgium’s CCB and Germany’s BSI both said patching and password changes are not enough for internet-exposed units. No exploitation of these six flaws is reported. - Midnight Blue (Nov 2026); Bytes Europe (13 Nov 2026, CCB warning); Cyber Press (13 Nov 2026); Insurance Journal, from Reuters (13 Nov 2026, BSI warning); Filstalexpress (13 Nov 2026, BSI firmware details) - CCB and BSI warnings 13 Nov 2026; research published Nov 2026

item.title: [High] ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens finds the exploited Node2Shell bug in SIMATIC SCADA and PCS 7, and more OT vendors confirm PHP2Shell exposure
item.category: Advisory — ICS Patch Tuesday (11 Nov 2026): Siemens (9 advisories, 10 flaws, two on Node2Shell), Schneider Electric SEVD-2026-314-01, Johnson Controls, Hitachi Energy and Phoenix Contact; CERT@VDE (8 advisories incl. Helmholz, Weidmüller, Beckhoff) and Axis CVE-2026-13312 (10 Nov)
item.description: Siemens published nine advisories on 11 November covering ten flaws, two of them describing how the exploited Node2Shell (Brotli) bug reaches its products. High-severity issues touch SIMATIC SCADA and PCS 7, SIMATIC WinCC Graphics Designer, meta-iot2050, ROS#, Simcenter Femap and the Mendix Studio Pro MCP server, and could allow code injection or system compromise. Several products have no fix yet and some versions will not be fixed, so Siemens points customers to mitigations; it has seen Node2Shell exploitation attempts but no attacks aimed at its products. Schneider Electric fixed a medium-severity file-handling flaw in EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody, Johnson Controls fixed EasyIO Neo IO Manager and a C•CURE 9000/victor installer that could expose admin credentials, and Hitachi Energy and Phoenix Contact confirmed PHP2Shell impact. A day earlier CERT@VDE flagged a dozen bugs in Helmholz’s myREX24V2 remote-access server (fix 2.21.0) and two PHP2Shell use-after-free flaws in MB connect line’s mbCONNECT24/mymbCONNECT24 remote-maintenance portal that allow unauthenticated code execution (CVE-2026-109618, CVSS 3.1 9.8; CVE-2026-109619, 8.1; fixed in 2.21.6), and Axis rated a Camera Station flaw 9.9 (CVE-2026-13312). - SecurityWeek ICS Patch Tuesday roundup (11 Nov 2026); Siemens ProductCERT; Schneider Electric SEVD-2026-314-01; CERT@VDE VDE-2026-141 and VDE-2026-128 (10 Nov 2026); Axis CVE-2026-13312 advisory (10 Nov 2026) - Published 11 Nov 2026 (Siemens, Schneider, Johnson Controls, Hitachi Energy); 10 Nov 2026 (CERT@VDE, Axis)

item.title: [High] N-central exploits now reach patched servers: attackers planted miners on 21 servers, 19 of them already running Hotfix 2
item.category: Active exploitation — N-able N-central: new 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell chains reported to work against Hotfix 2; miners found on 21 servers (13 Nov 2026); follows the 9 Nov “Able2Shell” dump of 33 flaws
item.description: On 9 November a researcher published “Able2Shell”, 33 flaws in N-able’s N-central remote monitoring and management platform with proof-of-concept code, and N-able shipped N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 the next day. The same researcher, Sean Bales, has since disclosed two new chains, 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, that he says work against the latest version; one uses a critical Apache Axis flaw, CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS 9.8). On 13 November Huntback reported cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2, mostly in the US, South Africa, Canada, the UK, Germany, France and Sweden, and Previdian described the attack path. N-able is restricting features, has turned off the Legacy API and Intune integration on hosted servers, and tells customers to upgrade Agents and Probes to 2026.4 HF1 or later and disable the Legacy API on premises, with more fixes coming. Many integrators manage plant-side Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment). - The Hacker News (13 Nov 2026, citing Huntback and Previdian); The Hacker News (12 Nov 2026, new chains); Tenable (Able2Shell FAQ, 10 Nov 2026); SecurityWeek (10 Nov 2026); N-able statements - Exploitation reported 13 Nov 2026; new chains disclosed 12 Nov 2026; Able2Shell disclosed 9 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] SonicWall SSL-VPN flaw that lets attackers skip SAML-enforced MFA is exploited and now in CISA KEV
item.category: Vendor advisory — SonicWall SonicOS SSL-VPN, CVE-2026-19868 (SAML/MFA enforcement bypass), Gen7 and Gen8 firewalls; reported exploited; added to CISA KEV, federal deadline 20 Nov 2026
item.description: SonicWall has fixed CVE-2026-19868, a flaw in how the SonicOS SSL-VPN service enforces authentication on Gen7 and Gen8 physical and virtual firewalls, after investigating a report of possible exploitation; CISA has added it to KEV with a 20 November deadline for federal agencies. Someone holding valid credentials for an alternate login method can bypass SAML, and any multi-factor authentication enforced through it. It is not an unauthenticated bypass, but it removes the control many sites rely on to make stolen passwords useless. Only devices with SAML enabled for SSL-VPN are affected: SonicOS 7.3.3-7015 and earlier, and 8.2.2-8015 and earlier. SonicWall VPNs are common at smaller utilities and plants and on vendor remote-access paths into OT (editorial assessment). - SonicWall PSIRT; CISA KEV; Help Net Security (9 Nov 2026) - Advisory and KEV addition reported 9 Nov 2026; federal deadline 20 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] Attackers are pushing rogue ScreenConnect clients through hijacked remote-support panels, reaching 288 endpoints at 48 organizations
item.category: Active campaign — rogue ScreenConnect clients pushed through hijacked cloud-hosted panels, detected 11 Nov 2026; ConnectWise advisory; Blackpoint ties the SCKit toolkit to KEV-listed CVE-2026-84869 (12 Nov)
item.description: Huntress reported on 12 November that, from the evening of 11 November, attackers used the Run Command feature in cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect panels to install rogue ScreenConnect clients and a toolkit it calls SCKit on at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations. The malware steals technicians’ session cookies, so a technician who connects to an infected machine can hand the attacker access to other customer sessions, letting it spread from client to client. Huntress suspects stolen credentials or hijacked sessions, and ConnectWise says it has found no compromise of its own infrastructure. Separately, Blackpoint Cyber said on 12 November that SCKit exploits CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9), a ScreenConnect flaw patched and added to CISA KEV in September, and that a fully patched client blocks its payload. No industrial victim is named, but many integrators and service providers support plant systems through ScreenConnect, so a compromised technician is a direct path into OT (editorial assessment). - Huntress (12 Nov 2026); Blackpoint Cyber via The Hacker News (12 Nov 2026); ConnectWise advisory; Sophos alert; The Hacker News (12 Nov 2026) - Activity detected 11 Nov 2026; reported 12 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] Comments close 30 November on NIST’s draft rewrite of its OT security guide, which adds water, food, rail, maritime and building-automation coverage
item.category: Guidance — NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 4 draft (released 21 Sep 2026); public comments close 30 Nov 2026; no CVE
item.description: NIST’s draft Revision 4 of SP 800-82, the US government’s main guide to operational technology security, is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The draft reorganises the guide around Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management now led by the Govern function, and adds sector material for building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and industrial IoT connected to cloud services. It also expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and detection, protecting system-management functions, and applying zero-trust principles. Many regulators, insurers and auditors use 800-82 as a reference, so its final wording can shape what operators are asked to show; the comment window is the chance for practitioners to flag guidance that would not work on a plant floor. - NIST CSRC, SP 800-82 Rev. 4 initial public draft (21 Sep 2026); SecurityWeek (24 Sep 2026) - Forward-looking: public comments close 30 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA launches an Installed Base Program to work with OT manufacturers on finding and securing their internet-exposed equipment
item.category: Program — CISA Installed Base Program (announced 10 Nov 2026); voluntary partnership with OT manufacturers; no CVE
item.description: On 10 November CISA announced the Installed Base Program, a voluntary partnership with original equipment manufacturers to identify internet-exposed OT devices across critical infrastructure and get them secured. The approach pairs what CISA sees on the internet with what manufacturers know about where their products are installed, so that owners can be warned sooner. Where it cannot tell who owns an exposed device, CISA says it may use administrative subpoenas to identify the owner. The launch follows weeks in which exposed refrigeration controllers were sabotaged at scale (see Incidents & Attacks). Operators should expect more direct notices, from CISA or their vendors, about equipment they may not know is reachable. - CISA Installed Base Program page; Industrial Cyber (Nov 2026); Viakoo Daily OT Security News via Security Boulevard (11 Nov 2026) - Announced 10 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] State utility regulators ask Congress to fund CISA, protect shared threat data and create a standards body for water cybersecurity
item.category: Policy — NARUC board resolution (adopted 11 Nov 2026) asking Congress to act on water-sector cybersecurity; no CVE
item.description: The National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, which represents state public utility commissions, adopted a resolution at its annual meeting on 11 November asking Congress to close CISA’s funding gap so it can keep supporting water and wastewater utilities, and to resource and strengthen WaterISAC. It also asks Congress to state in law that water utilities must share cyber-attack information with each other and with government, with that information exempt from public-records requests, and to authorise EPA to set up an independent, non-governmental Water Risk and Resilience Organization to develop minimum cybersecurity requirements. The resolution cites the attacks on water utilities in at least 12 states in July and August. It is a request, not a rule, but it puts the state regulators who approve utility rates, and so security budgets, on record behind baseline requirements. - Wolters Kluwer VitalLaw (12 Nov 2026); National Association of Water Companies statement via Water Online (12 Nov 2026) - Resolution adopted 11 Nov 2026; reported 12 Nov 2026
